```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>",
                      fig.width = 7, fig.height = 3.2, out.width = "100%",
                      dpi = 96)
has_ggplot2 <- requireNamespace("ggplot2", quietly = TRUE)
```

The **dependence** package offers three tools for studying the relation
between two variables $X$ and $Y$:

1. `indeptest()`, a test of independence based on the Bartlett statistic
   $B_n$ and the Pillai statistic $P_n$, which works for numeric, discrete
   and categorical variables alike;
2. `indepscan()`, an adaptive version of the test that scans the expansion
   order instead of fixing it in advance;
3. `depanalysis()`, which estimates the transformations of $X$ and $Y$ that
   make them as correlated as possible and draws them as *deformation plots*,
   showing what kind of dependence the test has found.

```{r setup}
library(dependence)
```

# The idea in brief

$X$ and $Y$ are independent if and only if every function of $X$ is
uncorrelated with every function of $Y$. The test replaces "every function"
with a finite family: an orthonormal basis $\phi_1, \ldots, \phi_p$ applied to
the ranks of $X$ and an orthonormal basis $\psi_1, \ldots, \psi_q$ applied to
the ranks of $Y$. Working on the ranks makes the procedure invariant to
monotone transformations of either variable. The bases are discrete
orthonormal polynomials (`basis = "poly"`, the default) or cubic B-splines
(`basis = "spline"`); a factor is represented through polynomial, spline or
dummy coding of its levels.

Let $\hat\lambda_1 \ge \cdots \ge \hat\lambda_r$, $r = \min(p, q)$, be the
sample canonical correlations between the two expanded data matrices. The
package computes

$$
P_n = n \sum_{s=1}^{r} \hat\lambda_s^2,
\qquad
B_n = -\left(n - \frac{p + q + 3}{2}\right) \sum_{s=1}^{r} \log\left(1 - \hat\lambda_s^2\right),
$$

the Pillai and Bartlett statistics. Under independence both converge to a
$\chi^2$ distribution with $pq$ degrees of freedom. When the orders are left
unspecified for numeric variables they are set to
$p = q = \max(1, \lfloor n^{0.31} \rfloor - 1)$, which grows slowly with the
sample size so that, as $n$ increases, the test gains power against any
form of dependence.

# Testing independence: $B_n$ and $P_n$

## Two numeric variables

A parabola is the textbook case in which correlation coefficients fail:
$Y$ depends on $X$ strongly, yet the two are nearly uncorrelated.

```{r parabola}
set.seed(123)
n <- 200
x <- runif(n, -1, 1)
y <- x^2 + rnorm(n, sd = 0.2)
cor.test(x, y, method = "spearman")$p.value
indeptest(x, y)
```

Spearman's test sees nothing, while both $B_n$ and $P_n$ reject
independence with p-values that print as zero. The result is a list, so
individual components can be extracted:

```{r components}
res <- indeptest(x, y)
c(B_n = res$B_stat, P_n = res$P_stat, df = res$p * res$q)
c(B_n = res$B_pvalue, P_n = res$P_pvalue)
```

The orders, the basis and the statistics to compute can be set explicitly.
With $p = q = 1$ the expansion contains only the linear function of the
ranks, and $P_n$ reduces to $n$ times the squared Spearman correlation:

```{r spearman}
r1 <- indeptest(x, y, p = 1, q = 1, test = "Pillai")
c(r1$P_stat, n * cor(x, y, method = "spearman")^2)
indeptest(x, y, p = 3, q = 3, basis = "spline")
```

Under independence the $\chi^2_{pq}$ approximation holds well already at
moderate sample sizes. Here is the rejection rate at the 5% level for two
independent variables with very different marginal distributions:

```{r size}
set.seed(1)
pv <- replicate(1000, {
  r <- indeptest(rnorm(100), rexp(100))
  c(B_n = r$B_pvalue, P_n = r$P_pvalue)
})
rowMeans(pv < 0.05)
```

## Categorical and mixed variables

The same function handles factors, as well as character and logical
vectors, which are converted to factors. For two factors the orders default
to the number of levels minus one; at that order every coding of the levels
spans the same space, and the Pillai statistic coincides with Pearson's
$\chi^2$ statistic for the contingency table:

```{r factors}
set.seed(2)
f1 <- factor(sample(c("low", "mid", "high"), n, replace = TRUE))
f2 <- factor(sample(c("A", "B", "C", "D"), n, replace = TRUE))
indeptest(f1, f2, basis = "dummy")
chisq.test(table(f1, f2), correct = FALSE)$statistic
```

A factor can also be tested against a numeric variable. Below, the
*spread* of $Y$, not its location, depends on the group, so a comparison of
means would miss the effect:

```{r mixed}
set.seed(3)
g <- factor(sample(c("a", "b", "c"), n, replace = TRUE))
z <- rnorm(n, sd = c(a = 0.5, b = 1, c = 2)[as.character(g)])
indeptest(g, z)
```

Integer vectors are treated as numeric, and each order is capped at the
number of distinct values minus one. With `ties = "average"`, which gives
tied observations a common rank, integer codes produce exactly the same
statistic as the corresponding factors with dummy coding:

```{r integer}
indeptest(as.integer(f1), as.integer(f2), ties = "average")$P_stat
indeptest(f1, f2, basis = "dummy")$P_stat
```

# The scan test

The fixed-order test commits to one pair $(p, q)$. If the dependence is of
high frequency, a small order may not capture it; if it is simple, a large
order wastes degrees of freedom. `indepscan()` evaluates the Pillai
statistic at every order $(k, k)$, $k = 1, \ldots, K$, converts each to its
null p-value $p_k$, and rejects when $p_k < c\,w_k$ for some $k$, with
weights $w_k$ and with the constant $c$ chosen so that the size is exactly
$\alpha$. Equivalently, the scan statistic is $\min_k p_k / w_k$.

The $K$ statistics are strongly correlated, so a Bonferroni correction
would be very conservative. Instead, the joint null distribution is
simulated. For continuous data without ties the statistics depend on the
data only through the ranks, so this null distribution does not depend on
the marginal distributions: one table, computed once for a given sample size,
serves every data set of that size.

```{r scan-null}
tab <- indepscan_null(n = 200, R = 2000, seed = 1)
tab$K
```

By default $K = \lfloor n^{0.31} \rfloor + 1$, two orders above the default
of `indeptest()`. We use `R = 2000` replications to keep this vignette
quick; the default `R = 2e4` gives a more accurate table and takes a few
seconds. Since tabulation is the expensive step, it is worth saving the
table with `saveRDS()` and reloading it later.

Consider an oscillating relation buried in noise:

```{r scan}
set.seed(9)
x <- runif(200)
y <- sin(5 * pi * x) + rnorm(200, sd = 1.2)
indeptest(x, y)
indepscan(x, y, tab)
```

At its default order, $p = q = 4$, the fixed-order test does not reject at
the 5% level, whereas the scan does. The profile shows where the evidence
lies: orders 1 to 5 give at most moderate evidence, while the statistic at
order 6, the first one flexible enough to follow the oscillation, is far
into the tail of its null distribution; `k.min` reports that order. It
describes where the dependence shows up and is not the result of a model
selection step: the p-value of the scan already accounts for having looked
at all orders.

Uniform weights make no assumption about the order at which the dependence
appears. Decreasing weights, such as the geometric weights
$w_k \propto 2^{-k}$, spend most of the level on low orders and therefore
favour monotone dependence. Weights can be changed without recomputing the
table:

```{r scan-weights}
sc <- indepscan(x, y, tab, weights = "geometric")
c(statistic = sc$statistic, p.value = sc$p.value)
```

The table is exact only for untied data. If `x` or `y` contain ties,
`indepscan()` warns that the p-value is approximate.

# Deformation plots

A rejection says *that* $X$ and $Y$ are dependent. `depanalysis()` shows
*how*. It computes the canonical variates behind the test: the pair of
transformations $(\hat g_1, \hat h_1)$, in the span of the two bases, such
that $\hat g_1(X)$ and $\hat h_1(Y)$ have the largest possible correlation
$\hat\lambda_1$, followed by further pairs, each uncorrelated with the
previous ones. Plotting $\hat g_s(x)$ against $x$ and $\hat h_s(y)$ against
$y$ gives the deformation plots: they show how each variable must be
reshaped to make the relation linear, and their shapes are often enough to
recognise the form of the dependence.

The plots are drawn with **ggplot2**, which must be installed. Without it
the transformations are still computed and returned in `$g` and `$h`.

## A conditional-variance relation

Here $X$ is the conditional standard deviation of $Y$. Correlation is zero
by construction:

```{r dep-v}
set.seed(2022)
n <- 500
x <- sqrt(rchisq(n, df = 2))
y <- rnorm(n) * x
cor(x, y)
m <- depanalysis(x, y)
m
```

The canonical correlations in `m$cor` are listed in decreasing order. The
first one, `r round(m$cor[1], 2)`, is the largest correlation that any pair of
transformations in the two spans can attain.

```{r dep-v-plots, eval = has_ggplot2}
m$plotx
m$ploty
```

$\hat g_1$ is increasing in $x$, while $\hat h_1$ is V-shaped around zero: the
relation that the first canonical pair linearises is the one between $X$
and $|Y|$, which is exactly the scale dependence that generated the data.
The scatter of the transformed pair shows the linearised relation, with the
fitted line having slope $\hat\lambda_1$:

```{r dep-v-xy, eval = has_ggplot2, fig.width = 4, fig.height = 3.2, out.width = "60%"}
m$plotxy
```

## Several modes of association

On a noisy circle, no single pair of transformations captures the whole
relation. The argument `dimensions` selects which canonical pairs to draw:

```{r dep-circle}
set.seed(2022)
th <- runif(n, 0, 2 * pi)
u <- cos(th) + rnorm(n, sd = 0.1)
v <- sin(th) + rnorm(n, sd = 0.1)
m2 <- depanalysis(u, v, p = 6, dimensions = 1:2, xlab = "u", ylab = "v")
round(m2$cor, 3)
```

```{r dep-circle-plots, eval = has_ggplot2}
m2$plotx
m2$ploty
```

Writing $u = \cos\theta$ and $v = \sin\theta$, the plots are easy to read.
In the first pair $\hat g_1$ is U-shaped and $\hat h_1$ is an inverted U:
up to scale they are $2u^2 - 1 = \cos 2\theta$ and $1 - 2v^2 = \cos 2\theta$,
two expressions of the same function of the angle. The second pair has the
W shape of the Chebyshev polynomial $8u^4 - 8u^2 + 1 = \cos 4\theta$ in both
variables, since $8v^4 - 8v^2 + 1$ is also equal to $\cos 4\theta$: a
weaker, higher-frequency mode of the same relation. The sign of each pair
is arbitrary, and the convention is to draw $\hat g_s$ rising at the right
end of the range of $x$.

The plots are ordinary ggplot objects and can be modified as usual, for
instance with `m2$plotx + ggplot2::ggtitle("Circle")`. The statistics shown
in the caption, Bartlett's by default, come from `indeptest()` called with
the same settings; use `annotate = "Pillai"`, `"both"` or `"none"` to
change them. The transformed observations and their basis coefficients are
returned in `$g`, `$h`, `$coef_x` and `$coef_y`, for further use.

# Summary

| Task                                          | Function                          |
|-----------------------------------------------|-----------------------------------|
| Test independence at a given order            | `indeptest(x, y, p, q)`           |
| Tabulate the null distribution of the scan    | `indepscan_null(n, K, R)`         |
| Test independence scanning orders $1,\ldots,K$ | `indepscan(x, y, null)`           |
| Visualise the form of the dependence          | `depanalysis(x, y, dimensions)`   |
